A year ago we launched Opus 4.5, the first model to write 100% of my code.

Shipping PRs hasn’t caught up, so today we’re launching Claude Ship in beta for Team and Enterprise. I use it all day every day and can’t imagine shipping without it. https://t.co/IfK0Oua6rZ

It multiplies my velocity. I don’t need to wait around for code review or babysit PRs, and the results are better.
Code Review looks for bugs, PR Steward works on fixes and failing checks, and Claude Approvals approves what your team’s policy allows (the last two are in beta).

Anyone can use /ship. If you’re on a Team or Enterprise plan, your admin can turn on Claude Ship per GitHub repo. I’d start with one repo and run Approvals in observe mode until you trust it.

https://t.co/p0T6zDSIwM

Introducing Claude Ship! 🚀 Claude can take a PR through review, fixes and an approval decision based on your team's policy.

If you've ever opened a PR, you know the flow: You open a PR and move on to your next task, then you get the review and you go back and fix something and you wait for the review to rerun and then you have to go find an approver. That's how it's designed to work: Most teams want a human to approve changes, and if you're writing code line by line, that's feasible. But many developers are already writing code with agents.

As the Claude Code team, we write most of our code with Claude. But we wanted post-PR to move just as quickly as the pre-PR part. Claude Ship evaluates your PRs, works on fixes, and determines when they can be merged based on policies that you define for your team. It is comprised of three components: Code Review (generally available): Performs a multi-faceted, in-depth review of a PR against your codebase. It collects findings, adversarially verifies them, classifies them, and posts comments on your PR.

You select from a tiered review depth for each repo: Quick, Standard, or Deep.

PR Steward (beta): Works to keep a PR green by responding to failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and comments from Code Review, other review tools, or reviewers. After every push it posts comments detailing what it did and how to revert those actions. You direct it with Claude comments or stop to have it step back. PR Steward is not designed to approve or merge PRs.

Claude Approvals (beta): Applies a policy that your team writes as a file in the repo. You can think of it as a smarter CODEOWNERS that approves routine changes autonomously if your policy allows it, or asks for human approval in specific situations. Claude can take into account Code Review findings and your own natural language classifiers. For most teams, we recommend starting in observe-only mode to gain confidence before enabling it as a required check in your branch protection configuration.

You can use Claude Ship in two ways: As a developer, upgrade your local CLI to the latest version of Claude Code and type /ship when you're ready to push a change.

Claude pushes the change, creates the PR, reviews it, and responds to feedback or failing checks. Whether the change can be merged is determined by your permissions and your repo's branch protection rules. As an admin or engineering lead, you can enable Claude Ship on a repo-by-repo basis and have it run automatically across your team's PRs. You turn on Code Review and PR Steward per repo, and Claude Approvals starts when a connected repo has a policy file on the default branch. You can leverage your existing branch protection and required checks.

You decide what review depth to use, when reviews run, and your spend limits, enabling a gradual rollout and pace of adoption.

Claude Ship is available for repos on GitHub on the Team and Enterprise plans. Costs are billed by tokens and will vary based on the number of PRs it touches, the review depth, and the effort put in by PR Steward. As an admin, you can set spend limits for Code Review and PR Steward.

Hope it's useful!

Agentic offensive frameworks like ARTEX are driving a surge in cloud intrusions. Wiz Research paired its telemetry with an operator's leaked logs and found noisy, machine-speed attacks that label their own work.

- Scope: ARTEX is open source with hundreds of forks, and others like Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike are in the wild too. "ARTEX" activity comes from unrelated operators, so it is not one campaign or actor. Since the Black October post, vendors have disclosed about twenty more related incidents, and Wiz's CIRT reports 3x the engagement requests.

- ARTEX-Harvester: tied at varying confidence to more than a dozen organizations between late October and mid-November 2026, clustered by a distinctive boto3 build, cross-victim incrementing Intent IDs and proxy pool overlap. Nearly every request came from a different residential or ISP exit, over 220 IPs at a single target, so IP blocking does little. The operator tried stolen creds, anonymous storage, sign-up and password-reset abuse, and identity-provider probing in parallel.

- One success chain: stolen VCS credentials opened private repos. The attacker created branches that abused CI workload identity trust, and harvest workflows dumped secrets and Terraform state. Separately, a stolen service-account token from an app pod could create privileged pods with the node root filesystem mounted. A "node-level collector" pod grabbed the kubelet PKI and every projected service-account token. The cert-manager token could read ArgoCD secrets, which led to cluster-admin.

- Both sides of one intrusion: an operator's open directory (over 3,000 files) matched the victim telemetry. Over four days in October the attacker hit two AWS accounts and seven EKS clusters. The chain ran from a stolen Terraform-runner session to a privileged pod and cluster-admin binding, then Jenkins RCE with a reverse shell. A pod escape dropped an ld[.]so.preload userland rootkit with a DNS-tunnel channel, disguised as a fontconfig service, with zero VirusTotal detections. Node, IRSA and Terraform-runner credentials were then used from the attacker's own server to read Terraform state and Secrets Manager and open SSM sessions.

- What the logs showed beyond telemetry: forged IdP admin tokens exposed 3,392 users and live sessions, beacons went to 19 hosts, and 50 SSH keys were pulled from a bastion database. The production Jenkinsfile was modified to run before its approval gate. CyberStrikeAI drove it, with csai- on nearly everything created (csai-escape pods, a csai-pentest-role IAM role, a csai-probe runner). Anthropic API keys were harvested from 50 hosts, and AI coding-assistant session histories were mined for SSO credentials. Separately, Censys counted over 1,400 exposed ARTEX consoles in early November.

- Self-labeling is the tell: pentest-recon user agents, pentest-* workspaces and pods, and a task counter like pentest-iNNNNNN. In-cluster, look for privileged container creation, nsenter, IMDS kube-env queries and drifted scripts reaching for cloud credentials. The report notes its rules are perishable as tools get renamed.

Takeaway: hunt your cloud audit logs and Kubernetes pod and workspace names for pentest-, csai- and the iNNNNNN counter. Check nodes for ld[.]so.preload entries and fontconfig lookalike services. Alert on EC2 or ECS task credentials used outside AWS, unusual GetCallerIdentity and mass secret value retrieval. Review CI branches that touch workload identity trust. Attacker IPs (for example the ARTEX operator hosts 68.68.250[.]114, 192.238.246[.]157 and 104.207.150[.]173) are in the report, and a CSV is in the wiz-research-iocs repository. The report lists the detection rule names too.

AIにDBのマイグレーションを任せると、0行一致でも「適用済み」と報告される穴がある。

@HimanshuRawal05 が指摘するPostgresの仕様だ。Claude CodeやCursor、Codexが条件を間違えたUPDATEを流してもPostgresは正常な結果として「UPDATE 0」を返すため、AIは適用完了と報告してしまう。

PostgreSQL公式ドキュメントのUPDATE項目でも、一致する行が0件のときはエラーとみなされずコマンドタグ「UPDATE 0」が返ると書かれている。statusやID、WHERE条件を間違えても正常終了に見える。

対策としてAIに証拠を出させる指示文が示されている。すべてのUPDATEとDELETEについて「正確なSQL」「Postgresが返した結果（例：UPDATE 42）」「想定行数」を示させ、実DBで実行していない場合は「UNVERIFIED」と書かせる。

本番へ流す前に非本番DBでBEGINとROLLBACKのトランザクション内で試して結果を見る。DEVの実務記事でも影DBでのドライラン、巻き戻せるかの確認や行数の差分チェックを重ねる安全策が共有されている。

もう一つ気をつけたいのが「UPDATE 500」のような数字の扱いだ。Postgresは値が元から同じだった一致した行も更新行数に数えるため、500件返っても500件の値が変わった証明にはならない。

DBのマイグレーションをAIに任せるなら非本番のBEGIN/ROLLBACKと証拠提示を条件にしたいところだが、普段はエージェントのSQL実行報告をどこまで確認している？

I uninstalled VS Code. Twice.

Some of my GitHub repos were hit by PolinRider, a supply chain attack that spreads through compromised npm packages.

It drops obfuscated JavaScript into your project, then injects a hidden task into .vscode/tasks.json that runs the moment you open the folder in VS Code or any fork like Cursor.

I ran the PolinRider cleanup script from OpenSourceMalware, cleaned my repos and removed VS Code. Everything looked clean.

Then I reinstalled VS Code, and strange activity from my machine showed up in my GitHub security logs again.

So VS Code went for good, and I switched to Zed. I was wary of its agent features since I'm not a vibe-coder, but so far I'm not going back. It opens from the CLI in 1.249s, it's minimal and customizable, and its plugin ecosystem is growing.

PS: If you use VS Code or a fork, check your projects for unexpected .vscode/tasks.json files. If you find one, rotate your GitHub tokens and SSH keys.
